messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh Tran was a 33-year-old married physical therapist who came to treatment after months of feeling as though his life had narrowed around a single violent morning. He had been driving home after an evening shift when another car ran a red light and struck his vehicle at high speed, spinning him into the median and pinning him in place while traffic rushed past. In the hours that followed, he was acutely aware of the force through his chest and back, the scrape of metal, and how helpless his body felt in the seat. Since then, he had come to believe that his body had been permanently damaged by what happened and that he could no longer trust his own body to protect him. He described feeling especially unsettled by loud noises, because a slamming door or sudden bang could carry him straight back to that moment in the wreck, and unwanted thoughts of the crash would arrive without warning, as if his mind were replaying the scene against his will. Waking from nightmares left him with a heavy residue of fear in the early morning, and those dreams made the accident feel close again, not safely over.

Those experiences quickly fed into a way of seeing the world that felt newly dangerous. Minh had become convinced that you can never know who will harm you, and after the crash he found himself noticing weapons or dangerous objects in nearly any environment, scanning parking lots, sidewalks, and even the therapy clinic lobby for anything that might be used against him. His attention was pulled away from patients and toward doorways, hands, and objects on carts, and he noticed that he was jumpy and easily startled whenever someone approached too quickly or a machine clanged in the gym. The more he watched for threat, the more danger he seemed to find, and each fresh jolt confirmed his sense that the world was less predictable than he had once assumed. At the same time, those moments of vigilance also sharpened his dread about his own body: a sudden startle, a tightness in his back, or a brief wave of dizziness could convince him again that he was still broken from the accident and that his body was unreliable under pressure. When he was on alert, the intrusive thoughts about the crash became more frequent, and the sound of a cart wheel hitting a threshold or a patient dropping a weight could pull him back into the memory with startling force.

Minh tried to manage this growing alarm by cleaning and organising things repeatedly to feel in control, straightening the home bathroom, rearranging supplies at work, and checking his surroundings over and over before sessions began. He also mentally rehearsed worst-case scenarios to feel prepared, imagining where he would move if a stranger came in angry, how he would protect his wife, or what he would do if his back gave out in front of a patient. For a while, these routines gave him a sense that he was doing something useful, but they also kept his mind fixed on danger and made him even more watchful. The more he scanned for threats and ran through disasters, the more readily he spotted possible weapons, the more easily he was startled, and the harder it became to concentrate long enough to finish notes or stay fully present with patients. He found himself rereading charts and losing track of conversations, then becoming more frustrated with himself and more certain that his body and attention were no longer dependable. That sense of unreliability pushed him back into the same habits of cleaning, checking, and rehearsing, because uncertainty felt unbearable.

Over the following months, Minh’s life at home and at work became arranged around avoiding reminders and staying prepared. In the clinic he chose treatment rooms near exits, and in the evenings he would return home and methodically clean the kitchen counters or sort the garage tools before he could sit down with his wife. He knew these habits made him feel briefly steadier, but they also left him tense and exhausted, as if he were always bracing for another impact. The nightmares, the unwanted crash thoughts, and the bursts of fear at loud noises had become common enough that he no longer trusted ordinary routines to remain ordinary. What finally brought him to seek help was the growing strain on his marriage and his fear that he was teaching himself to live as if danger were everywhere. He was most afraid that one day his body would fail him again at work or on the road, and most hoping that he might learn how to step out of that constant scanning long enough to feel safe with his wife and patients again.
